title: The Wise Men of Chelm, the Watchman and the Fur Coat
summary: Chelm's night watchman is cold, so the town elders decide: a fur coat! But every morning brings a new problem, and every evening they decide on a funnier solution: a fur coat worn inside out, a horse for the watchman, a horse in the synagogue... until the cantor himself climbs onto the horse and sings from the saddle. A rhyming story based on a folk tale of the Wise Men of Chelm.
pages:
At night in Chelm the watchman marched with a lantern in his hand,
guarding all the shops, and he was cold — the coldest in the land!
"Brrrr!" shivered the watchman. "I'm freezing! I'm cold as can be!"
"What will we do?" everyone asked. "Let's think... let's think... maybe...? Let's see!"

So the town elders gathered, the rabbi at their head, and nobody disagreed,
and they decided all together — that was the way, the tradition, indeed.
But each decision that looked like a great success
brought, the very next morning, a brand-new surprise mess!

The elders gathered: "A fur coat for the watchman, big and warm!"
The watchman put it on and said, "What a comfort in a storm!"
But the next day the officer came, with a mustache, and shouted, "Fur?!
Only ministers wear fur! What nerve! How dare you, sir!"

The elders gathered: "We'll turn the coat inside out — fur on the outside, leather in!"
The watchman wore it that way, and looked like a sheep — from his toes to his chin.
And the next day the watchman came: "Last night a skinny little wolf came by,
thought I was a sheep, and followed me till I could hardly breathe — oh my!"

The elders gathered: "The watchman will ride a horse, strong and tall!
Then the wolf will look up and say, 'Ugh... he's way too tall!'"
And the next day the watchman came, the horse beside him with sad, sad eyes:
"He has nowhere to sleep! No stable! No shed of any size!"

The elders gathered: "The great synagogue! There's room there, and it's warm!"
So the horse tiptoed in on its hooves and stood there, cozy and safe from harm.
But the next day the worshippers came and found a horse among the pews,
they gave it a push — it got frightened, and trotted out lightly, clip-clop in its shoes.

The elders gathered: "Stand the horse by the prayer stand — there's an empty space!"
So the gabbaim set it there, and it stood like a king, calm and full of grace.
But the next day the cantor came, in his robe, his mustache sad and wide:
"There's a horse at the prayer stand! And me? There's no room for me — oy, it hurts inside!"

The elders gathered: "The cantor will ride the horse — right there, inside!"
And the cantor was happy, and his eyes smiled a smile so wide.
They pushed from below, they pulled from above, and the cantor — hop! — went up,
and sat straight in the saddle, proud and handsome, without a single hiccup.

Clop, clop, clop — went the horse, with the cantor singing on its back,
in a big, deep voice — and all Chelm sang along, right on track.
And ever since, that's the custom in Chelm, to this very day:
a cantor on a horse — and Shabbat shalom, they say!

And the little wolf sat by the window in the cold, cold snow,
and his tummy rumbled every time: "Grr-grr-grr!" — growling low.
Then Gitele smiled and tossed him some challah — and he ate it, and sang, sweet and slow.

And at night the watchman made his rounds on the horse, with a lantern in his hand,
in his inside-out fur, the horse swaying gently — and he was toasty warm and grand.
"Brr," said the watchman, "it's still a little bit cold!"
And Yokel banged his hammer: "Let's gather! Let's gather! Quick — the elders, young and old!"
